item.title: The Makkah defense pact and Bangladesh: A test of strategic autonomy
item.description:
From the Middle East to South Asia, the strategic map is changing rapidly. Prolonged wars, regional conflicts, economic uncertainty, and intensifying rivalry among major powers are prompting states to rethink how they secure their national interests.
One of the most significant recent developments is the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, signed in Makkah on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan. The agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three, while also calling for broader defense cooperation.
For Bangladesh, the issue is no longer merely whether it should join the Makkah framework. The larger question is how Dhaka can develop a defense and foreign-policy strategy that maximizes its security options without becoming strategically dependent on any single power or drawn into conflicts unrelated to its national interests.
Recent statements from Bangladesh indicate that Dhaka is keeping the possibility of participation open. Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir has said that Bangladesh views the possibility positively but would consider any such arrangement in light of its national interests and the changing global environment. This is not the same as a decision to join, but it makes the strategic debate increasingly relevant.
More than an “Islamic NATO”
The Makkah agreement has understandably been described in some quarters as an emerging “Islamic NATO.” Such a description, however, is premature. NATO possesses a highly developed institutional structure, integrated command arrangements, and decades of operational experience. The Makkah framework is at a much earlier stage.
Nevertheless, its political and strategic significance should not be underestimated. Saudi Arabia contributes enormous financial resources and considerable geopolitical influence; Türkiye brings a sophisticated and increasingly autonomous defense industry, NATO experience and advanced capabilities in drones, electronic warfare, and other military technologies; while Pakistan contributes a large and experienced military and nuclear capability.
The agreement therefore brings together three complementary sources of strategic power. If implemented effectively, it could eventually facilitate greater cooperation in defense production, military training, intelligence, technology transfer, and collective deterrence. Türkiye's foreign minister has also indicated that the pact is not directed against any particular country and that other states could potentially participate in the future.
Why now?
The emergence of the Makkah framework must be understood against a rapidly deteriorating regional security environment. The Israeli strike on Hamas leadership in Doha in 2025 demonstrated that even states traditionally viewed as relatively secure could find themselves exposed to the spillover effects of regional conflicts. Qatar, an important mediator between Israel and Hamas, condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty.
The subsequent escalation of regional tensions, including the 2026 Iran-related conflict and attacks affecting Gulf security, has reinforced the perception among regional powers that they cannot rely indefinitely on external security guarantees.
The Makkah initiative can therefore be interpreted partly as an effort to strengthen regional strategic autonomy. It does not necessarily represent a rejection of the United States or existing alliances. Rather, it reflects a broader trend in which regional powers seek greater capacity to manage their own security environment.
What could Bangladesh gain?
Bangladesh has legitimate reasons to examine the development carefully. Its defense capabilities remain significantly dependent on imported equipment and technology. Türkiye's growing defense industry could provide opportunities in drones, unmanned systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, and defense manufacturing. Saudi Arabia offers financial strength and investment potential, while Pakistan has extensive military experience and established institutions for military education and training.
Bangladesh already maintains separate relationships with all three countries. Saudi Arabia is important to Bangladesh because of labour migration, remittances, investment, energy, and broader political and cultural ties. Türkiye is becoming an increasingly important economic and defense partner. Relations with Pakistan remain historically sensitive because of the legacy of 1971, but contemporary diplomatic, economic, educational, and military contacts have expanded.
A carefully designed engagement with the Makkah framework could therefore offer Bangladesh three potential advantages:
But these benefits must be weighed against substantial risks.
Bangladesh's security environment is different
The principal weakness of simply joining an existing security framework is that Bangladesh's security priorities are not identical to those of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, or Pakistan.
Saudi Arabia's primary security concerns are centred on the Gulf and the wider Middle East. Pakistan's strategic calculations are deeply influenced by India, Afghanistan, and South Asian military competition. Türkiye's security environment encompasses Europe, the Black Sea, the Middle East, and its NATO commitments.
Bangladesh's priorities are different: Relations with India, the Bay of Bengal, the situation in Myanmar and Rakhine, border security, maritime trade routes, the Indian Ocean, and emerging climate-related security challenges.
Consequently, Bangladesh should not automatically adopt another country's threat perceptions as its own.
This distinction is particularly important because of the collective-defense provision. If Bangladesh were to become a formal member of a pact under which an attack on Pakistan could potentially trigger obligations toward Pakistan, India's assessment of Bangladesh's strategic orientation would inevitably change. Defense cooperation with Türkiye is one thing; participation in a collective-defense arrangement involving Pakistan is strategically much more consequential.
Managing India, China, and the United States
India would naturally watch any Bangladeshi move toward the Makkah framework closely. Bangladesh therefore needs to avoid creating the perception that its defense policy is being directed against India.
China would also have strong reasons to monitor developments. Pakistan is one of Beijing's closest strategic partners, while China maintains substantial economic and diplomatic relations with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia. Bangladesh itself is an important Chinese economic and defense partner. Greater Bangladeshi diversification of defense relationships could therefore encourage Beijing to strengthen rather than reduce its engagement with Dhaka.
Washington would view the development through the wider lens of the Indo-Pacific. Bangladesh's strategic location along the Bay of Bengal makes its foreign and defense policies relevant to maritime security and the wider Indo-Pacific balance.
This is where Bangladesh's diplomatic skill will be tested.
From weapons buyer to technology partner
The most important lesson for Bangladesh is that defense diplomacy should not be reduced to purchasing weapons.
Buying fighter aircraft from one country, drones from another, and missiles from a third may diversify suppliers, but it does not necessarily create strategic autonomy. Bangladesh could remain a permanent consumer in the global arms market.
A more ambitious objective would be to acquire technology, production capability, and knowledge.
Bangladesh should explore joint development and local production of drones and unmanned systems, military electronics, surveillance equipment, communications systems, and selected naval technologies. Cooperation with Türkiye could be particularly valuable in this regard. Defense-industrial cooperation can also stimulate research, skilled employment, technological innovation, and broader industrial development.
The strategic question should therefore change from “Where can Bangladesh buy weapons?” to “How can Bangladesh become a partner in developing and producing defense technology?”
A better option: Diversified defense diplomacy
For Bangladesh, the most realistic strategy may be diversified and issue-based defense cooperation rather than membership in a rigid military bloc.
Dhaka can deepen defense-technology cooperation with Türkiye; expand investment, training and maritime-security cooperation with Saudi Arabia; maintain selective military education, training, and peacekeeping cooperation with Pakistan; continue appropriate defense and technological cooperation with China; pursue maritime surveillance and advanced technological cooperation with the United States and European partners; and maintain pragmatic security cooperation with India on border management, maritime affairs, counterterrorism, and regional stability.
Such an approach would maximize Bangladesh's options while minimizing dependence.
Three principles should guide any future defense agreement.
First , Bangladesh should avoid joining a military alliance explicitly directed against another state.
Second , Bangladeshi territory should never become a foreign military base or a platform for military operations against another country.
Third , Bangladesh should avoid excessive dependence on any single country's weapons, technology or defense infrastructure.
A fourth principle is equally important: Before entering any major security agreement, Bangladesh must assess not only the immediate military benefits but also the economic costs, diplomatic consequences, and potential obligations that could arise during a future conflict.
Strategic autonomy, not strategic isolation
The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement could become an important new element in the security architecture of the Middle East and the wider Muslim world. Whether it remains a limited trilateral arrangement or evolves into a broader regional framework is still uncertain. What is clear, however, is that the agreement has opened a new strategic conversation.
Bangladesh should therefore watch the initiative closely rather than rush toward membership. If a formal proposal for participation emerges, Dhaka should evaluate its precise obligations, military benefits, economic costs, and diplomatic consequences before making a decision.
Bangladesh's national interest would not be served by entering an arrangement in which another country's war automatically becomes Bangladesh's war.
The country's strategic objective should instead be strategic autonomy without strategic isolation.
Bangladesh's greatest strategic asset is not a fighter aircraft, missile, or military alliance. It is geography. Situated at the intersection of South Asia and Southeast Asia and facing the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh occupies a position of exceptional strategic importance.
If that geographical advantage is combined with effective diplomacy, economic strength, technological capacity, and credible national defense, Bangladesh can become not a follower of another country's security architecture but an influential regional actor in its own right.
The goal, therefore, should not be to choose one camp over another. It should be to build a network of partnerships in which different countries cooperate with Bangladesh in different areas, while Bangladesh retains the freedom to determine when, where, and how its national interests require engagement.
Dr Nasir Uddin Ahmed is a retired Major, researcher and political/security analyst. Email: directtoradmin2007@gmail.com .

item.title: Transforming Chittagong’s port capacity
item.description:
The planned $550 million Laldia Terminal is one of the most ambitious port projects Bangladesh has taken on - one that has the potential to reshape Chittagong.
A modern terminal with expanded capacity, efficient cargo handling, and improved connectivity is exactly what we need to keep pace with rising export volumes and global shipping demands. Above all else, this is what we need as Bangladesh looks to take the meaningful next step in its development journey.
Done right, this could become a cornerstone of Bangladesh’s economic future, but ambition alone is not enough. We have seen too many large infrastructure projects suffer from delays, cost overruns, and coordination failures. The Laldia Terminal cannot afford to join that list.
Given that the port is projected to be made entirely with foreign investment, there is an even greater need to ensure this is done right. Foreign investment continues to be a challenge for our nation, and ensuring the port development stays on track is one way to instil confidence into future investors.
As such, this project must be executed with discipline: Strict adherence to timelines, transparent procurement, and rigorous oversight.
Moreover, future development for Bangladesh must be built upon the principles of sustainability, with a clear operational plan that ensures projects deliver the benefits promised.
If implemented properly, the terminal will strengthen Bangladesh’s position in global supply chains, support export‑led growth, and ease the strain on existing port facilities. It is a project that can genuinely transform Chittagong -- but only if it is treated with the urgency it deserves and not yet another slow‑moving development scheme.
Bangladesh needs this terminal. Now it must prove it can deliver it -- on time, on budget, and with the seriousness our future demands.

item.title: Promises on e‑rickshaw regulation mean nothing without action
item.description:
The government moving to bring e-rickshaws under a policy framework, with systematic licensing and registration planned through local government, is unquestionably a positive development - on paper.
However, Bangladesh has heard this promise before.
For some time now, authorities have announced plans to register, regulate, and reorganize these vehicles, only for the initiatives to stall, fade, or be quietly abandoned.
This time, the country needs more than statements. It needs implementation.
E‑rickshaws are now an essential part of Bangladesh’s transport ecosystem and play a significant role in providing affordable mobility in addition to creating livelihoods for hundreds of thousands. None of this has ever been disputed.
Yet, their rapid, unregulated growth coupled with their high-risk has also created serious problems. Untrained drivers should never have been allowed to operate these vehicles, and it is no wonder that Dhaka has seen increased traffic chaos and more frequent accidents.
Without proper oversight, a mode of transport that should help communities has unfortunately ended up putting them at risk, not to mention worsen our traffic woes.
The government’s renewed commitment to registration, route management, and safety standards is therefore welcome - but credibility depends entirely on follow‑through.
We expect the government to realize why past attempts failed and not give in to coercion from vested interests resisting change. Unless these structural issues are addressed, this latest initiative will meet the same fate.
Bangladesh cannot afford another cycle of announcements without action. E‑rickshaws are here to stay and the goal now is to transform them from the source of disorder they are today to becoming a safe, integrated part of the transport system.

item.title: The uncomfortable truth for young men
item.description:
Looking out from behind a senior sub editor’s desk after 14 years in newsrooms, I often catch myself watching the latest wave of SSC and HSC candidates celebrating their results.
They smile for photos, full of idealism and relief, unaware of the silent shift waiting just around the corner.
Every time I see them, my mind wanders back to the young boy I once was -- standing in those exact same shoes, making the exact same dangerous assumptions about time, money, and responsibility.
If I could reach back through the decades, pull my younger self aside, and spare him from the quiet stumbles of my youth, this is the unvarnished truth I would tell him.
Look at how softly the world treats you right now. You make mistakes, and people smile.
You fail, and you are offered grace.
But listen to me carefully: That cushion is about to evaporate.
Society will soon measure your worth not by your good intentions, but by your utility and the weight of your pocket.
I made the mistake of assuming that affection was permanent. It isn't.
A jobless, directionless man -- a bekar purush -- commands no real respect, whether in extended family circles, among peers, or in the wider world.
Three anchors you cannot ignore
I spent years prioritizing the wrong things in the wrong order. If you want to build a life that stands firm when storms hit, you need three things, strictly in this order:
Build these three early, and you will step miles ahead of the crowd.
There were times when I saw people taking shady shortcuts, wondering if sticking strictly to pure means was keeping me behind. It was a lie.
Anyone who tells you that you cannot build substantial wealth through halal avenues is merely justifying their own moral compromises.
The real battle you will face isn't finding halal work -- it is having the discipline to turn down fast, attractive opportunities.
Walk away from every questionable deal, no matter how tempting.
‘Later’ is the biggest lie you will tell yourself
I used to tell myself: "I'll focus on earning after A Levels," and then, "I'll worry about real skills after university." That hesitation cost me years.
A framed certificate is not a magic key. No employer, no investor, and no client is going to hand you money simply because you held up a degree on graduation day.
If you wait until you finish institutional milestones to start learning how the real world works, you are already dangerously late.
Start gaining practical knowledge today. Tomorrow is an illusion.
Degree is not a strategy
Look closely at the university graduates around you. How many of them actually achieved their dreams solely because of the paper they received?
Now sit in the chair I sit in today -- as a team leader.
If two people walk into my office for a position, and one spent four years reading outdated theory while the other spent four years building real-world skills and executing projects, I will pick the practitioner every single time.
Unless you are becoming a doctor or an engineer, do not treat a degree as your core strategy.
Value comes from execution, not enrollment.
I used to think that life required choosing between worldly success and spiritual devotion. That was a false dichotomy.
Getting married and building a home seems daunting in our culture, but it becomes effortless when you build yourself into a trustworthy, responsible, and stable man.
I have seen wealthy men who neglect their prayers and indulge in corruption; society uses them for money but despises their character. On the flip side, I have seen bright young men stay in the mosque all day, possessing beautiful manners, yet unable to spare Tk100 for a necessity because they refused to build a livelihood.
Be gentle and approachable, but stay firm when your principles are tested.
Your physical and mental window is closing
Right now, you think you have infinite time. You don't. Today, you are labeled a "student."
Almost overnight, that label shifts to "unemployed."
At 14, 18, or 20, your energy is a superpower.
You can sleep four hours, learn a complex skill, work a shift, and recover instantly.
A few years down the line, that raw stamina wanes, your cognitive processing slows, and life demands higher stakes for every error.
The world forgives a teenager's mistakes; it penalizes an adult for the exact same ones.
Use your peak energy right now while the stakes are low and the grace period is still open.
Achieving something at 21 hits entirely differently than achieving it at 31.
When you achieve independence early, society notices. The doors open wider, and the trajectory of your entire life shifts upward.
Protect your name at all costs
In 14 years of professional life, I have seen careers built on reputation and destroyed by the lack of it. Your name is your currency.
Be the young man in your neighborhood, among your friends' parents, and in your institution who is known as safe, reliable, and honourable.
A reputation takes years of quiet consistency to build and seconds of foolishness to ruin.
The formula is simple: High skill, clean income, excellent manners, and absolute reliability.
If you say you will do something, do it -- no excuses.
If there is one profound lesson my career in media has hammered into me, it is this: Speed of execution beats perfection every single time.
If you decide today to learn a skill, do not plan for next month -- start the foundation before the sun sets today.
If you want to build a public voice or a service, have your first draft, post, or offer live within hours.
Move fast. Moving fast means you fail faster, learn faster, and correct course faster.
I wasted too much time waiting for the "right moment" or waiting for life to change on its own.
Life never changes on its own. You have to grab the steering wheel and force the turn yourself.
Stop waiting. Your future self depends on what you do before you go to sleep tonight.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Mirza Fakhrul’s real test will come in 2031
item.description:
When the Constitution of Bangladesh was amended in 1991 and the parliamentary system was reinstated, the then interim president is said to have made an interesting observation.
Seeing that virtually all the powers of the president had been taken away by the amendment, Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed remarked: “The president will now have no other work to do except visit the shrines.”
However, it cannot be said that all presidents have been able to visit shrines peacefully.
In Bangladesh’s deeply divided political landscape, a deceased leader is sometimes feared more than a living one.
In 2002, the BNP forced its own nominated president, Badruddoza Chowdhury, to resign after only seven months in office. His crime? He had expressed a desire to visit the grave of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Some say, however, that president Chowdhury had expressed reluctance to visit the grave of former president Ziaur Rahman, the founder of the BNP.
Whatever the truth, Badruddoza Chowdhury had to leave Bangabhaban in disgrace amid the controversy over which grave he would or would not visit.
The present is not free of controversy either.
Many had expected the new Parliament to do two things at the beginning of its session: Establish an upper house with 105 members, and then elect a new president through a vote of the members of both houses.
The debate over how members of the upper house would be elected, according to the proportion of votes received in the general election or the proportion of seats won in the lower house, ended with the BNP’s absolute victory.
Meanwhile, some significant changes to the powers of the president are also expected, if the “July Charter” is indeed a meaningful document for the BNP.
Caretaker is coming
However, even before all this, a new president was elected on August 20.
There has hardly been any adverse reaction to the person elected.
It would not be wrong to say that Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir is one of the most experienced and respected politicians not only in the BNP but also in Bangladesh.
He visited the grave of Ziaur Rahman but expressed no desire to visit the grave of Bangabandhu. He has passed the initial test of survival. But the discussion over the future of the presidency has not ended with this election, it may only have begun.
Why Awami League-nominated Md Sahabuddin remained president for six months even after the BNP secured a two-thirds majority in the election is also a matter of curiosity and deserves analysis.
There is little doubt that Mirza Fakhrul’s work as president will largely be limited to formalities. But even if the president has nothing to do for the next four and a half years except “visit the shrines,” the final six months will be eventful.
Under the current system, elections must be held within 90 days before the expiry of Parliament’s term. In other words, Parliament remains in session during the election.
But the High Court has already reinstated the system of holding elections under a non-partisan, impartial caretaker government. All that remains is to determine the process for selecting the chief adviser and other members of the caretaker government and to incorporate the necessary amendments into the Constitution.
In principle, Bangladesh’s 2031 general election will be held under a caretaker government.
Biswas to Iazuddin
A feature of the caretaker system is that the prime minister will request the president in writing to dissolve Parliament only after the existing Parliament has completed its full five-year term.
The government will also resign, and the chief adviser of the caretaker government will take the oath of office and begin work.
The president will play a major role during this period, as he will be the only elected officeholder, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and the wheels of the bureaucracy will turn on his orders.
Here, one can look back to 2001.
Justice Latifur Rahman made 13 secretaries OSD within an hour of taking office as chief adviser on July 15.
His move created a stir in political circles. There was strong suspicion within the Awami League, the party that had just left power, that Justice Rahman would work against it.
But the fact is that the new chief adviser sidelined secretaries appointed by the Awami League in order to work impartially. He did not do this alone. He acted in consultation with the then president, Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed.
Two other instances can be recalled. First, Justice Habibur Rahman took over as chief adviser after the caretaker system was introduced in 1996. But when Army Chief General Mohammad Nasim tried to seize power, some senior officers helped President Abdur Rahman Biswas at Bangabhaban foil the coup attempt.
Second, in 2006, the ruling BNP tried to secure a chief adviser of its choice by increasing the retirement age of judges. After this attempt to manipulate the caretaker system failed, BNP-nominated President Iazuddin Ahmed declared himself chief adviser.
Many suspected at the time that President Ahmed was acting in consultation with the recently departed prime minister, Khaleda Zia. But that attempt to influence the election also failed when Iazuddin Ahmed, under pressure from the army, declared a state of emergency and postponed the election.
Md Sahabuddin’s disrespect
Against this diverse and turbulent backdrop, Mirza Fakhrul will face a test of impartiality and integrity. The country’s next election will be held within three months of the end of the 13th Parliament.
Those three months will be the most important and consequential period of Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir’s presidency.
The date of the presidential election, the 20th of this month, appears to have been carefully chosen. The respect Tarique Rahman showed President Md Sahabuddin does not appear to have been mere courtesy.
Sahabuddin once complained that the chief adviser of the interim government had shown him no respect at all and had instead humiliated him. He wanted to resign at the time. But, overwhelmed by Tarique Rahman’s respect, he remained in office.
Six months later, the BNP government forced President Md Sahabuddin to resign. There did not appear to be much respect on display then. He was not even invited to the swearing-in ceremony of the new president.
With the presidential election taking place six months after the formation of Parliament, Mirza Fakhrul’s term will expire in August 2031. That means he will remain in this crucial position throughout the entire election period under the caretaker government.
What kind of role will he play? Can he rise above his loyalty to the party and play a neutral role in the interests of the country?
Mirza Fakhrul’s answer is “yes.”
He has resigned from all BNP posts and announced that he has severed his ties with the party. He has said that he will now act impartially.
Maladaptive political culture
It is certainly reassuring to hear Mirza Fakhrul’s words, and ordinary people will hope that he can act accordingly.
But they also know how difficult it is to play a genuinely “neutral” role in Bangladesh’s bitter and vindictive political culture.
For example, it is practically impossible to deny Sheikh Mujib’s place in Bangladesh’s independence struggle and political history. But will Mirza Fakhrul be able to acknowledge this truth in any of his speeches? If he can, it will be a sign of his political wisdom and maturity -- and, perhaps more importantly, that of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
People will not expect the impossible from the president. No one will expect him to go beyond his constitutional limitations and perform some miracle.
They will simply expect the president to make it easier for his chief adviser to uphold the central principle of the caretaker government system, ensuring a free and fair election.
However, it is also true that no president has so far been able to overturn an election. Since the caretaker system was incorporated into the Constitution, three elections have been held under this arrangement.
Two were conducted under BNP-nominated presidents, and Khaleda Zia’s party was defeated in both.
The election held under an Awami League-nominated president resulted in disaster for Sheikh Hasina.
What the situation will look like in 2031, however, is difficult to predict.
Sabir Mustafa is former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.description:
We have made our micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) the egg-laying, wool-bearing, milk-giving pig -- the German fantasy animal that does everything at once.
We want them to give jobs to men, women, and people with disabilities. We want them to go green, though the market pays no premium for going green. We want them to sell at the lowest price while their rent, raw materials, and transport costs all rise. We want them to transact with the bank, pay taxes.
Then we complain that the MSMEs are informal. But we fail to address the concern that formality raises production costs while the shelf price stays the same.
We bring them to seminars. We pat their backs. We give them awards. And every seminar opens with the same sentence: MSMEs do not have access to credit. And that cycle goes on for decades. We leave the ground hostile yet ask these small firms to carry the country to a trillion dollars.
We must be living in a fool’s paradise.
The situation however could be improved and MSMEs can indeed be a conduit to the trillion dollars hope.
But the MSMEs will not be able to do it alone. They can do it if we see MSMEs and large businesses as a nexus and in the same value creation network.
A food safety certification costs the same whether you sell to one shop or five hundred. So does a cold chain, a compliance officer, a brand, a gas connection, a distribution network. These are fixed costs.
A large firm spreads them across enormous volumes while a firm turning over Tk50 lakh a year cannot spread them at all. So when a cost shock arrives, it does not land equally. It irritates the large firm. It kills the small one.
That is the story of the last 11 years. The charts tell it.
Sources: BBS price indices; Energy Division fuel notifications; BERC orders; Bangladesh Bank. Marketing and gas are charted on a separate scale. Values for 2026 are estimates; dashed segments are projected.
Since 2015, rent has risen 93%. That is the CPI housing group, since Bangladesh publishes no commercial rent index. Producer prices for raw materials are up 64%, diesel 63%, electricity for business premises 61%. Industrial gas has risen more than five times. Marketing has risen more than nine times.
Now reflect: How much has the price gone up on the bag you bought last month from a boutique on Facebook? Zero, or close to it.
Look at how fast it arrived. Diesel rose 42.5% in a single night on August 6, 2022. Gas for large industries rose 150% in one order on February 1, 2023, from about Tk 11 to Tk 28 per cubic metre.
The retail electricity tariff rose again on June 1, 2026, and the small-industry tariff rose 18.3% against a system average of 16.7%. The small firm was charged above the average.
Source: Energy and Mineral Resources Division and BPC price notifications, 2015–2026, verified against reporting in Dhaka Tribune, The Daily Star, Prothom Alo, The Business Standard.
Sources: BERC gas tariff orders, 2017–2025, and BERC and Power Division electricity tariff orders, 2015–2026.
One number deserves far more attention. Industrial gas costs Tk 30 per cubic metre for an existing user. For a new user it costs Tk 40. We charge the entrant a third more than the incumbent. We say we want new firms to emerge and inefficient ones to make way. Then we put a price on entry.
Marketing tells the same story. In 2015 it cost Tk 30 to reach a thousand people on Facebook. By 2022 it was Tk 98. Today it is Tk 280.
Roughly Tk 65 of that is Bangladeshi VAT and withholding tax. Much of the rest is the fall of the taka. Only a fraction is Meta raising its price.
Since Covid-19, hundreds of thousands of MSMEs built their businesses on f-commerce. Their cost of finding a customer has risen ninefold while the price they charge has barely moved.
Sources: LightCastle Partners, Digital Marketing Landscape Bangladesh 2015; agency benchmark studies, 2022 and 2026; Bangladesh Bank FE Circular No. 04 of 8 May 2023.
So where has the money gone? The consumer pays far more than she did a decade ago. The producer does not receive it. What sits between them has widened: Transport, storage, spoilage, tolls, layer upon layer of trading, and the VAT and duty increases of January 2025.
When we discuss inflation, we take the side of the consumers; but barely we think of the producers who are also choking to death. The producer and the buyer are not opponents. They are two ends of the same rope.
This is why consumers should worry about the small firm. As MSMEs thin out, the cheapest supply goes first. The neighbourhood producer, the small trader, the one-room manufacturer who kept the price honest.
Fewer sellers mean less competition, and less competition means the consumer pays more.
I was sitting recently with the chief executive of one of our largest agro-logistics companies. He was explaining their struggle to source and sell rural produce in their urban outlets.
The cold storage network in Bangladesh is old and was built for potatoes; so the company cannot use it for perishables. Despite the investment in highways, congestion remains.
Recently they tried an innovative scheme to source fresh sweet from the South and sell it in outlets in Dhaka. Half the fresh-milk sweets became stale on arrival.
I can write a book on my experience in trying to solve these supply chain challenges. I remember in 2010, we wanted to promote crates to cut post-harvest losses on pineapple shipped from the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
The crown took up nearly half the cargo space and bruised half the load. And when the load spoiled, the trader pushed the loss down to the small farmer.
In a chain without contracts, loss flows downhill until it reaches whoever has the least power to refuse it.
It does not have to work that way though. Between roughly 2006 and 2016, large numbers of cattle were distributed to char dwellers in the northern districts. It soon became clear there was no high-yielding fodder.
The next round of interventions built the fodder system and then the artificial insemination system. Later, the sheer volume of cattle resulted in processing capacity. A system formed.
But notice how it formed. One missing piece at a time, over a decade. It became a system only when a large buyer appeared at the end of it.
That is what Bangladesh is missing. Our policy imagines large and small enterprises as rivals. It treats the corporate sector as something the MSME must be shielded from, and the MSME as something to be supported separately: Its own ministry, its own foundation, its own seminar.
The two never meet. The small firm faces the market alone. It buys at the worst price in the chain, sells at the worst price in the chain, and absorbs every shock that is passed down.
Bangladesh does not need thousands of grocery shops each bargaining alone against a fragmented wholesale market. It needs them inside networks.
This is the road our neighbours took, and they did not leave it to chance.
In Vietnam, the Ministry of Industry and Trade partnered with Samsung to build a domestic supplier base, sending engineers into Vietnamese factories to bring them up to standard.
More than 300 Vietnamese firms now sit in Samsung's supplier tiers. Malaysia has run a Vendor Development Program for decades, registering anchor companies, matching them with small vendors and financing those vendors through a dedicated bank window.
In Thailand, more than 10,000 7-Eleven outlets trade. Most are franchised to individual owner-operators who buy through one system rather than a hundred.
In Indonesia and the Philippines, millions of warungs and sari-sari stores are the exact counterparts of our mudir dokan . Supply platforms now give these one-room shops something close to the buying price of a chain.
In none of these countries did the small shop close. It stopped standing alone, and networked small firms carried those economies upward.
How can we fix this?
The MSMEs in Bangladesh will deliver the trillion-dollar economy. But they cannot deliver it in the arrangement we have built for them: A few million firms, each operating alone, each absorbing every shock the system passes down, each competing against the large enterprise that ought to be its customer.
However, if we put the small and the large enterprises in the common nexus of creating value, the trillion-dollar hope will arrive soon.

Can we ever have safer roads?
item.description:
That the Road Safety Foundation reported that at least 438 lives were lost in crashes across Bangladesh in June alone no longer surprises us, nor elicits any strong response. This is what we have been reduced to, when hundreds of lives lost every month have become so commonplace that the nation collectively barely registers it.
Behind each number lies a family shattered and a community scarred. But most of all, every month, we are reminded that as a nation, we continue to fail to protect citizens on the roads.
The causes are painfully familiar: Reckless driving, unfit vehicles, weak enforcement, and poor infrastructure. Year after year, probes are announced, awareness campaigns launched, and promises made.
Yet the death toll never budges. Road safety in Bangladesh has long been a crisis, yet we seem to be drifting further away from doing something about it.
Despite the public marching in 2018, and despite numerous calls for overhaul, what we continue to lack is structural reform. There remains woeful licensing standards, no mandatory vehicle fitness checks, and no effort to ensure genuine enforcement of traffic laws.
All of this points back to our culture of impunity. Too often, powerful transport owners and reckless drivers escape accountability, undermining justice. Road safety cannot improve until violations carry real consequences.
Bangladesh’s roads should not be death traps, yet they continue to be. Every life lost is a reminder that safety should not be optional but a right for every person in this country.

item.title: Preparing for the inevitable
item.description:
That Bangladesh is likely to face flooding in July and August, according to forecasts, should not be a surprise. We have long known that our geography and climate, in addition to the adverse effect of climate change, make floods inevitable for our nation.
What remains surprising, and unacceptable, is how often we remain unprepared despite knowing what is coming.
Floods, beyond being natural events, have long been a test for our governance. Each year, families lose homes, crops are destroyed, and livelihoods are disrupted.
Each year, relief arrives, but too late and too little. The cycle of damage and recovery continues, while prevention and preparedness remain neglected.
Suffice to say, this is not a solution.
Preparedness must begin before the waters rise. From strengthening embankments to clearing drainage systems to ensuring shelters are stocked and accessible. From mobilizing local authorities to identify vulnerable communities to coordinating evacuation plans.
In addition, we must also ensure that relief funds are transparent and reach those who need them most, rather than being lost to corruption or inefficiency.
Technology and data must also play a crucial role. Early warning systems must be expanded and communicated effectively, not buried in bureaucratic channels.
Simultaneously, we need more investment in resilient infrastructure across the country, from roads, schools, and hospitals, where they are needed most, not where the most headlines are generated.
Bangladesh has lived with floods for centuries, but living with them should not mean suffering from them. Preparedness is cheaper than recovery, and prevention saves lives. The government must treat the coming floods not as an annual inconvenience but as a national priority.

item.title: Receiving our fair share from the carbon market
item.description:
The government's decision to strengthen Bangladesh's carbon market marks an encouraging step towards aligning economic development with environmental responsibility.
As climate change continues to intensify, countries must look beyond conventional environmental policies and embrace market-based mechanisms that reward sustainable practices, while discouraging excessive emissions.
For a climate-vulnerable nation like Bangladesh, such initiatives are not merely desirable but increasingly necessary: A well-functioning carbon market can attract investment, encourage cleaner technologies, and provide businesses with incentives to reduce their carbon footprint.
It also has the potential to unlock new sources of climate finance, helping fund renewable energy, conservation projects, and other low-carbon initiatives.
If implemented effectively, it could strengthen Bangladesh's position in global climate negotiations while contributing to long-term economic resilience.
However, ambitious announcements alone will not deliver meaningful results. Clear regulations, transparent monitoring, and strong institutional capacity will be integral to building a credible carbon market.
Emissions data must be accurate and independently verified, while enforcement mechanisms should ensure that participants comply with established standards.
Policymakers must also engage industries, financial institutions, and environmental experts throughout the process to design a practical and trusted system.
It is also important to ensure that the carbon market complements broader climate action. Expanding renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, protecting forests and wetlands, promoting sustainable transport, and encouraging climate-smart agriculture must remain central pillars of national policy.
Public awareness will also be crucial, as businesses and citizens alike need to understand both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with a low-carbon economy.
Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its commitment to addressing climate challenges, despite contributing only a small share of global emissions. Strengthening the carbon market reflects that commitment and deserves recognition.
We must now translate this intent into action -- through consistent policies, effective implementation, and unwavering political will.
The success of this decision will depend on the discipline we display to see it through.

item.title: Building a modern public transport system
item.description:
That Dhaka’s metro rail will begin operating up to Kamalapur in April 2027 is certainly welcome news.
Once completed, the extension will connect the capital’s busiest railway station with the country’s first metro line, making travel faster, more convenient, and better integrated for countless commuters.
This is another important step towards building a modern urban transport system that Dhaka has desperately needed for decades. Test runs are expected to begin in January, with work on the extension now well advanced.
The real challenge now, however, is in ensuring that the project reaches the finish line exactly as promised.
Bangladesh has seen too many infrastructure projects suffer from repeated deadline extensions, escalating costs, and unnecessary administrative delays, and the Kamalapur extension must not become another example of that.
Authorities should maintain strict oversight, ensure transparency in procurement and implementation, and resolve any remaining technical issues without compromising quality or safety.
Delivering the project on schedule and within budget would strengthen public confidence and demonstrate that major infrastructure can, indeed, be completed efficiently.
At the same time, this extension should not be viewed as the end goal; Dhaka's growing population and worsening traffic congestion demand a far broader transformation of public transportation.
The metro rail alone cannot solve the city's mobility crisis: Other planned MRT lines, bus rapid transit systems, commuter rail improvements, and better integration between buses, trains, and metro services must all move forward without losing momentum.
At the same time, reliable pedestrian access and affordable fares must be prioritized for more people to embrace public transport over private vehicles.
While the progress towards Kamalapur deserves recognition, it should also reinforce the urgency of completing the wider vision.
Bangladesh must continue investing in efficient, accessible, and sustainable public transportation -- because the economic, environmental, and social benefits will far outweigh the costs for generations to come.
